clue.text: It's said to be decided

definitions.meaning: spoken aloud or uttered, as a word is articulated
marked or definite, as in a decided preference

explanation.surface: Someone notes that a matter has, by report, been settled.
explanation.definitionFit: A word that is uttered has been voiced; a strong, unmistakable accent or tendency is called decided or marked.

clue.text: Become exhausted after dismissal

definitions.meaning: to run short, be used up completely
in cricket, a batsman put out by the wicket being broken while running

explanation.surface: A batsman is worn out after being sent back to the pavilion.
explanation.walkthrough: Cricket: a run-out is a way a batsman is dismissed, when fielders break the wicket before the batsman completes a run.
explanation.definitionFit: Supplies that are used up have been depleted; in cricket the run-out is a standard mode of dismissal.

clue.text: Diet seen to be bad for the most destitute

indicators.note: bad suggests the letters of the two words are spoiled and rearranged

explanation.surface: A poor diet is judged harmful for the very poorest people.
explanation.walkthrough: 'bad' shuffles the letters of DIET SEEN.
explanation.definitionFit: Destitute people are in great want, so the most destitute are those in greatest need.

clue.text: Dreadful pain? Opt out to some extent

indicators.note: dreadful signals that the letters of the following words are mangled into a new order

explanation.surface: Someone in terrible pain wonders whether they can partly opt out.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Dreadful' rearranges the letters of PAIN OPT OUT.
explanation.definitionFit: A phrase meaning partially or within limits, a synonym of the qualifying expression.

clue.text: Harmonize in a musical group

definitions.meaning: to agree or be in accord with, as a verb
an ensemble of instruments, especially early music such as viols

explanation.surface: Players are urged to blend their sound within an ensemble.
explanation.definitionFit: To be in accord with is the verb sense; an Elizabethan ensemble of viols or recorders was a noun sense of the same word.

clue.text: In the meadow no thistle, for instance, can be seen

indicators.note: in means the letters lie inside the run of words meadow no

explanation.surface: A field is described where no weeds such as thistles are visible.
explanation.walkthrough: 'thistle, for instance' is a loose definition: thistle seeds carry soft fluffy filaments, the stuff of thistledown.
explanation.definitionFit: Thistles produce fluffy seed tufts, a soft fibrous material named for its likeness to feathers.

clue.text: Punishing run providing a challenge

definitions.meaning: a punishment in which the offender runs between two lines of people striking out
a glove thrown down as a challenge to fight

explanation.surface: A gruelling run is presented as a test to be taken up.
explanation.definitionFit: Running between rows of attackers was a military punishment; a knight's glove cast down was a formal dare.

clue.text: Send home notes about the country in Italy

indicators.note: about means the two notes surround the next piece

parts.note: re and te are two notes of the sol-fa scale
patria is the Italian word for homeland or country

explanation.surface: Someone sends musical scores home concerning a land in Italy.
explanation.walkthrough: One word 'notes' supplies two separate notes, RE and TE, placed either side of PATRIA.
explanation.definitionFit: Returning a person to their native land is exactly sending them back to their own nation.

clue.text: Not in office, a grand exile starts a period without power

parts.note: a party not in government is out
G is a common abbreviation for grand, a thousand

indicators.note: starts means only the opening letter of exile is taken

explanation.surface: An ousted politician, now a grand exile, begins a time without authority.
explanation.walkthrough: 'period without power' reads as political powerlessness but means an electricity cut.
explanation.definitionFit: A cut in electricity supply, a blackout, is a time when the mains is down.

clue.text: The record is still in!

parts.note: a best-ever mark not yet bettered, read alongside a cricket batsman still in, not out at the innings' end

explanation.surface: Excited news that a sporting best still stands.
explanation.walkthrough: In cricket a batsman who is still in when the innings ends is described with this word, as is a record no one has topped.
explanation.definitionFit: A record never surpassed has not been defeated, and a not-out batsman likewise was never dismissed.

clue.text: Go astray loudly on one note in a piece of music

parts.note: to sin is to stray morally
F, forte, is the musical marking for loud
I is the Roman numeral one
A is one of the musical notes

explanation.surface: A player wanders off course by playing too loud on a single note in a piece.
explanation.definitionFit: An Italian term for a symphony or an orchestral overture, a kind of instrumental composition.

clue.text: In a manner of speaking, left out to become an eyesore

indicators.note: out means the letter for left is dropped from the word

parts.note: style is a way of expressing oneself

explanation.surface: Someone's way of talking, missing something, becomes unsightly.
explanation.walkthrough: 'eyesore' is literal here: a sore on the eye.
explanation.definitionFit: A painful swelling on the eyelid is quite literally a sore of the eye.

clue.text: Vigorously rehabilitate heartless Tory — warts and all

indicators.note: rehabilitate suggests rebuilding the letters into a fresh order
heartless means the middle of tory is removed, leaving its first and last letters

explanation.surface: A call to reform a mean Conservative politician, flaws included.
explanation.walkthrough: 'heartless' leaves TY from TORY; 'rehabilitate' shuffles TY with WARTS and ALL.
explanation.definitionFit: Acting stoutly and resolutely, with sturdy strength, is acting with vigour.

clue.text: Fastidious individual

explanation.surface: A fussy person is described.
explanation.definitionFit: Fussy people are choosy; a specific, single item is singled out from the rest.

clue.text: Mood that's peremptory

explanation.surface: A commanding temper is described.
explanation.definitionFit: In grammar the command form is a verb mood; an urgent, compelling demand admits no refusal.

clue.text: The French in retreat leave one country for another

indicators.note: leave means those letters depart from the first country

parts.note: Australia is the first country

indicators.note: in retreat means the French article is read backwards

parts.note: la is the French feminine word for the

explanation.surface: French troops falling back abandon one nation for another.
explanation.walkthrough: 'in retreat' turns LA into AL, which 'leave' removes from AUSTRALIA. 'another' is the definition: another country.
explanation.definitionFit: The result is a second nation, the central European republic with Vienna as capital.

clue.text: Formal arrangement, prescribed by the King, perhaps

parts.note: a set text is one prescribed
the king is a chess piece

explanation.surface: A ceremonial layout is ordered by the monarch.
explanation.definitionFit: A carefully staged scene or composition in fixed form is a formal, prearranged display.

clue.text: Almost ghostly coloured bands

indicators.note: almost means the word is cut short by its final letter

parts.note: spectral means like a ghost

explanation.surface: Faint, phantom-like stripes of colour appear.
explanation.definitionFit: Light split by a prism shows rainbow-like stripes of colour, the plural of the scientific term.

clue.text: It brings round the cases left after a drinking party

indicators.note: after means the letter for left follows the party

parts.note: a carouse is a drunken revel

explanation.surface: Someone collects luggage abandoned following a boozy night.
explanation.walkthrough: 'cases' are suitcases at an airport baggage reclaim, where a rotating belt delivers them.
explanation.definitionFit: At airports a rotating conveyor belt returns luggage to passengers.

clue.text: The culprit finally got sharply rebuked, it's understood

indicators.note: finally means just the closing letter of culprit is used

parts.note: wigged is British slang for scolded severely

explanation.surface: The guilty party was at last scolded, and the point is grasped.
explanation.walkthrough: To 'wig' someone is dated British slang for giving them a dressing-down.
explanation.definitionFit: Informal British slang for grasping or realizing something.

clue.text: Keep vigil first at the Barbican, perhaps

indicators.note: first means the vigil word goes in front

parts.note: a watch is a period of keeping vigil
a keep is a castle's strong tower

explanation.surface: Stand guard first at the London arts complex.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Keep vigil' looks like one verb phrase; 'Keep' is the castle stronghold. A barbican is a fortified gateway or outer tower; London's Barbican takes its name from one.
explanation.definitionFit: A barbican is a defensive outwork, often a tower from which guards look out.

clue.text: Unusual choice

explanation.surface: An odd selection is described.
explanation.definitionFit: Something seldom found is uncommon; choice goods are of fine, excellent quality.

clue.text: Express criticism about the outlook

parts.note: re means about or concerning
a view is an outlook

explanation.surface: Someone voices disapproval of the forecast.
explanation.definitionFit: A critic writes a critical appraisal of a book or show.

clue.text: Description of the weather reported to be prevailing?

indicators.note: reported means the word is heard rather than read

parts.note: raining describes wet weather

explanation.surface: A forecaster's report says the wet weather is dominant.
explanation.definitionFit: A ruling monarch holds sway, so a dominant condition is said to be ruling or holding sway.

clue.text: One of five in "This happy breed of men, this little world"

definitions.text: One of five in "This happy breed of men, this little world"

parts.words: One of five in "This happy breed of men, this little world"
parts.note: the Shakespeare line from Richard II is a pentameter, five metrical feet of unstressed then stressed syllables

explanation.walkthrough: The quotation is John of Gaunt's speech in Shakespeare's Richard II, written in pentameter: five feet per line.
explanation.definitionFit: A metrical foot of a short then long syllable, five making a pentameter line.

clue.text: Obtains support when contradicted

parts.note: gains means obtains
aid means support

explanation.surface: Someone receives help even while being argued against.
explanation.definitionFit: To deny or speak against a claim, an old-fashioned synonym.

clue.text: My clue transformed the Aristotelian school of philosophy

indicators.note: transformed means the letters of my clue are changed into a new arrangement

explanation.surface: A setter boasts their clue has reshaped Greek philosophy.
explanation.walkthrough: 'transformed' rearranges the letters of MY CLUE.
explanation.definitionFit: Aristotle taught at a gymnasium near Athens named after Apollo Lyceus, giving its name to his school.

clue.text: Plot to have peers as companions

parts.note: a bed is a garden plot
fellows are peers or equals

explanation.surface: A scheme to make the nobility one's associates.
explanation.definitionFit: People sharing a bed, figuratively allies or associates.
